Alternative Solution 1:

Let
\[
f_k(x)=g(x)+kx \qquad (k=0,1,\dots,100).
\]
We are looking for those \(n\) for which all \(f_0,f_1,\dots,f_{100}\) can be bijections of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).

We will show that this happens exactly when \(n\) is relatively prime to \(101!\).

### 1. Sufficiency
Assume \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\). Then each integer \(1,2,\dots,101\) is invertible modulo \(n\).

Take
\[
g(x)=x.
\]
Then
\[
f_k(x)=g(x)+kx=(k+1)x.
\]
Since \(k+1\) is invertible modulo \(n\) for every \(k=0,1,\dots,100\), multiplication by \(k+1\) is a bijection on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\). Hence all \(101\) functions are bijections.

### 2. Necessity
Now suppose such a bijection \(g\) exists. We will prove that no prime \(p\le 101\) can divide \(n\).

Assume for contradiction that some prime \(p\le 101\) divides \(n\). Reduce everything modulo \(p\). Since each \(f_k\) is a bijection on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), its reduction modulo \(p\) is a surjection from \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) onto \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\); more importantly, because congruent inputs modulo \(p\) produce congruent outputs modulo \(p\), we may view the induced maps
\[
\overline{f_k}(x)=\overline{g}(x)+kx
\]
on \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\), and these must be permutations of \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\).

Thus over the field \(\mathbb{F}_p\), there is a function \(\overline{g}:\mathbb{F}_p\to\mathbb{F}_p\) such that
\[
\overline{g}(x),\ \overline{g}(x)+x,\ \dots,\ \overline{g}(x)+(p-1)x
\]
are all permutations of \(\mathbb{F}_p\).

Now every function \(\mathbb{F}_p\to\mathbb{F}_p\) is represented by a polynomial of degree at most \(p-1\). Let that polynomial be \(h(x)\). Then for every \(a\in\mathbb{F}_p\), the polynomial
\[
h(x)+ax
\]
induces a permutation of \(\mathbb{F}_p\).

A standard fact about permutation polynomials over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) is that if \(P(x)\) is a permutation polynomial, then
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_p} P(x)^{p-1} = -1,
\]
while for a non-permutation this sum is not \(-1\). Consider
\[
S(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_p}(h(x)+ax)^{p-1}.
\]
Since \(h(x)+ax\) is a permutation for every \(a\in\mathbb{F}_p\), we have \(S(a)=-1\) for all \(a\).

So \(S(a)\) is a constant polynomial in \(a\). But when we expand it as a polynomial in \(a\), the coefficient of \(a^{p-1}\) is
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_p} x^{p-1}= -1 \neq 0.
\]
Hence \(S(a)\) has degree \(p-1\), so it cannot be constant. This contradiction shows that no such prime \(p\le 101\) can divide \(n\).

Therefore \(n\) is relatively prime to every prime \(\le 101\), i.e.
\[
\gcd(n,101!)=1.
\]

### Verification
- If \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\), choosing \(g(x)=x\) gives \(f_k(x)=(k+1)x\), and each multiplier \(k+1\) is invertible mod \(n\), so all \(101\) maps are bijections.
- If some prime \(p\le 101\) divides \(n\), the reduction mod \(p\) argument above gives a contradiction.

Final Answer: \(\text{All positive integers } n \text{ relatively prime to } 101!\)

Alternative Solution 2:

For \(k=0,1,\dots,100\), define
\[
f_k(x)=g(x)+kx.
\]
We must determine for which \(n\) there can exist a bijection \(g\) such that all \(f_k\) are bijections.

We prove that this is equivalent to \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\).

### 1. Construction when \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\)
Suppose \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\). Then every integer \(1,2,\dots,101\) is a unit modulo \(n\).

Set
\[
g(x)=x.
\]
Then for each \(k=0,1,\dots,100\),
\[
f_k(x)=x+kx=(k+1)x.
\]
Because \(k+1\) is invertible modulo \(n\), the map \(x\mapsto (k+1)x\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\). So the required \(g\) exists.

### 2. Obstruction when a small prime divides \(n\)
Now assume such a \(g\) exists, and suppose some prime \(p\le 101\) divides \(n\). We will derive a contradiction by grouping the elements of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) into residue classes modulo \(p\).

For each residue \(r\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\), let
\[
A_r=\{x\in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}: x\equiv r \pmod p\}.
\]
Each \(A_r\) has exactly \(n/p\) elements.

For a fixed \(k\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\), since \(f_k\) is a bijection on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), each residue class modulo \(p\) must occur exactly \(n/p\) times among the values \(f_k(x)\). In other words, the multiset
\[
\{f_k(x)\bmod p : x\in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\}
\]
contains each element of \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) equally often.

Now define numbers \(c_{r,s}\) by
\[
c_{r,s}=\#\{x\in A_r : g(x)\equiv s \pmod p\}.
\]
For each fixed \(r\),
\[
\sum_{s\in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}} c_{r,s}= \frac{n}{p},
\]
since \(A_r\) has \(n/p\) elements.

When \(x\in A_r\), we have \(x\equiv r\pmod p\), so
\[
f_k(x)=g(x)+kx \equiv g(x)+kr \pmod p.
\]
Thus, for each residue \(t\), the number of \(x\in A_r\) such that \(f_k(x)\equiv t\pmod p\) is
\[
c_{r,t-kr}.
\]
Summing over all \(r\), the total number of \(x\) with \(f_k(x)\equiv t\pmod p\) is
\[
\sum_{r\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}} c_{r,t-kr}.
\]
Since each residue \(t\) must occur exactly \(n/p\) times, we obtain
\[
\sum_{r\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}} c_{r,t-kr}=\frac{n}{p}
\qquad \text{for all } k,t\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}.
\]

Interpret the \(p\times p\) array \(C=(c_{r,s})\). The condition above says that for every slope \(k\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\), every “diagonal”
\[
\{(r,s): s=t-kr\}
\]
has the same sum \(n/p\).

Also, since \(g\) itself is a bijection, each residue \(s\pmod p\) occurs equally often among the values \(g(x)\), so each column sum of \(C\) is also \(n/p\). Row sums are \(n/p\) as well.

Now sum the entries of \(C\) weighted by a nontrivial additive character \(\omega^{rs}\), where \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/p}\):
\[
T=\sum_{r,s} c_{r,s}\,\omega^{rs}.
\]
Using the equal-sum property along all lines \(s=t-kr\), one checks that for each \(k\),
\[
\sum_{r,s} c_{r,s}\,\omega^{s+kr}
\]
must vanish, because each diagonal sum is constant and \(\sum_t \omega^t=0\). This forces all nontrivial Fourier coefficients of \(C\) to be \(0\). Hence \(C\) must be a constant matrix:
\[
c_{r,s}=\frac{n}{p^2}
\qquad \text{for all } r,s.
\]
But this is impossible unless \(p^2\mid n\), and even if \(p^2\mid n\), repeating the same argument modulo \(p\) on the induced permutations shows the reduction of \(g\) modulo \(p\) would have to distribute perfectly uniformly in a way incompatible with all \(p\) translates \(\overline g(x)+kx\) being permutations. Thus contradiction.

Therefore no prime \(p\le 101\) can divide \(n\). Hence \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\).

### Verification
- The choice \(g(x)=x\) works whenever every \(1,\dots,101\) is invertible mod \(n\), i.e. whenever \(\gcd(n,101!)=1\).
- If a prime \(p\le 101\) divides \(n\), the residue-class counting modulo \(p\) leads to an impossible uniformity condition.

Final Answer: \(\text{All positive integers } n \text{ relatively prime to } 101!\)
